resources.string: Describe the room: its size, the rows and columns of seats, and what the walls and floor are made of. You can also load a sample room to explore.
Find out how clearly people can hear at each seat. You clap at the front while the phone listens at a few seats, then it checks the background noise.
After measuring, you\'ll see which seats can follow the speaker, and whether echo, noise or distance is the problem.
Try cheap changes before spending money: curtains, switching off fans, moving the speaker or using a microphone. ClearRoom predicts how much each one helps.
Leave the phone in the room to see how background noise changes through the day. Only sound levels are kept, never audio.

Good morning, everyone. Today we will look at how sound travels in this room. Please listen carefully, and raise your hand if any word is hard to hear. When we speak to a class, our voice has to reach the back row as clearly as the front. Let us find out how well it does.

Where the grey noise bar reaches the voice bar, that pitch is drowned out. The numbers show how far the voice is above the noise; 15 dB or more is comfortable.

Height and colour show how clearly each spot can hear. The white line marks where listening becomes easy (0.60). Drag sideways to turn, pinch to zoom.

The curve is the clap fading away; the straight line is the fit that gives the echo time, over the shaded range. The closer they match, the more you can trust the number.
Do a clap test on the Measure tab to see how the sound dies away.

At speech pitches the echo lasts about %1$s s, within the %2$s s a classroom should have.
Low pitches ring longest: thick panels or soft furniture help most.
Mid pitches ring longest: curtains or soft boards help most.
High pitches ring longest: even thin curtains help.
Faded bars are borrowed from the nearest pitch: the claps were too weak there.
Each ridge is one pitch fading after the clap; longer ridges ring longer.
Speech is a rhythm of loud and soft. Each line shows how much of it reaches this seat at one pitch (1 = all of it). Echo pulls the lines down on the right; noise pulls them all down.
At %1$s, about %2$d%% of the speech rhythm survives at 1 kHz.
